definition: Merriam-Webster's Word of the Day for November 7, 2026 is: abandon &#149; \uh-BAN-dun\&nbsp; &#149; noun Abandon refers to a feeling or attitude of wild or complete freedom. // The two friends spent the work week looking forward to hitting the clubs together on Friday night and dancing with total abandon . // After years of contemplating, he finally decided to make a career pivot and pursue his passion with reckless abandon . See the entry > Examples: “That experience didn’t just provide her the freedom to fail; it pushed her to take risks with abandon and follow her instincts. Even if that movie wasn’t well-received, it was an ambitious project that she had an obvious passion for.” — Coleman Spilde, Salon , 5 July 2026
did_you_know: ? Given the familiarity of the verb abandon , you may associate the noun with the act of leaving and never returning. But despite being a relative newcomer to English, the noun abandon , with its more pleasant connotations of freedom, is likely here to stay. It only entered the English language in the early 1800s, as a borrowing from French that goes back to an Old French word meaning “surrender.” (English had borrowed the verb abandon centuries before from the French speakers living in medieval England.) Louisa May Alcott recognized the word’s utility; she used it of Jo in Little Women , writing that “when the writing fit came on, she gave herself up to it with entire abandon, and led a blissful life, unconscious of want, care, or bad weather ...”
